newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian court to rule on Rao plea on Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Indian court to rule on Rao plea on Wednesday.

text.p: An Indian court will decide on Wednesday whether to accept a request by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao for legal protection against arrest in a criminal forgery case, court officials said.

On Monday, Delhi High Court Judge S.K. Mahajan deferred a ruling on the request, which Rao's lawyers lodged last Friday immediately after a court issued a warrant for the arrest of the former Congress party leader.
Federal police have charged Rao and five others with using forged documents in 1989 to defame a rival politician. Rao, who quit as Congress leader last month, has not commented publicly on the case.
Last week Rao won a temporary reprieve by requesting anticipatory, or pre-emptive, bail, which amounts to legal protection against arrest.
After a two-hour hearing on Monday, Judge Mahajan told a packed courtroom that he would rule later on the request.
If the High Court rejects Rao's request, he was expected to appeal to the Supreme Court. If detained, Rao would be put in custody pending a hearing on the forgery case set for October 14, they said.
Rao's lawyers said the former Prime Minister needed legal protection against arrest as he suffered from diabetes and heart trouble.
Rao, already the first former prime minister to be formally charged with criminal offences, would become the first ex-prime minister to be taken into custody.

The turmoil within Congress, which has led India for all but four years since independence in 1947, has rocked financial markets, which anticipate trouble for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark index fell more than three percent on Monday. In mid-session trade on Tuesday, the index was down 13.03 points, or 0.43 percent, to 2,989.83.

On Monday the Supreme Court reserved judgement on a request by police that a hearing into a separate criminal cheating case be shifted from a crowded local courtroom to a more secure location. It was expected to rule later this week.
Until the High Court and Supreme Court pass judgement on the two requests, Rao will be spared arrest.

A lower court has scheduled a hearing for Wednesday in the cheating case. At the hearing Rao was scheduled to be charged with criminal conspiracy to cheat an expatriate businessman of $100,000 in 1983. Rao says he is innocent.
The government asked that the hearing, which looked likely to be delayed, be moved to a cavernous government conference hall where security forces could protect Rao.
But until the Supreme Court rules on the request, Rao will not have to appear in court over the cheating case.
The Supreme Court said on Monday that both the cheating and forgery cases should preferably be concluded within three months of their start.
